statements.text: Hi! Priya here, 34. I rent a tiny 1BHK in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, fifth floor, no lift, my calves are legendary.
Staff nurse, ICU, Manipal Hospital. Mostly night shifts. Six years in.
Red Activa, 2016 model, rattles like a tin of coins but it gets me to work.
Biscuit is my ginger cat. He's three and has decided the flat belongs to him.
I'm vegetarian. Always have been. Eggs are my one grey area, don't tell Amma.
Filter coffee, two cups a day, no sugar. Do not speak to me before cup one.
Tuesday and Thursday mornings I do yoga at a little studio on 12th Main, right when my night shift ends.
Been with Arjun for two years now. He's an architect, annoyingly tidy. I am not.
Sundays I'm at my boyfriend's flat in Jayanagar for dosa breakfast. Non-negotiable.
My partner and I each put 20k into a joint account every month, house deposit fund.
My sister Divya lives in Pune, she's a pharmacist at Ruby Hall.
Malayalam at home, Hindi and English from school, Kannada from living here. I can scold in all four.
Phone is a Redmi Note 10. Batery gives up by 4pm, every single day.
Biscuit weighs 6.2 kg now. Vet said diet. Biscuit disagreed.
Brought home a tiny black kitten from the clinic car park. Named her Soot. Biscuit is furious.
Saving up for a master's in critical care nursing, hopefully starting 2027.
Back from Kochi, my cousin's wedding. Three days of sadya, I may never eat again.
First week at Fortis done. Honestly the ICU there is calmer than Manipal ever was, and nobody rings at 4am asking me to cover.
Got the Pixel 8a last week. The Redmi is in a drawer where it can think about what it did.
Arjun and I broke up. It's been coming for months. I'd rather not talk about it yet.
Doctor says my iron is rock bottom so I'm eating chicken now. Three decades of veg, undone by haemoglobin.
Swapped my Activa for an Ather electric scooter. The old girl went to my neighbour's son.
Palpitations after the shifts, so it's green tea only now. Filter coffee, I will miss you.
Started French on Duolingo, want to order croissants in Paris without pointing.
Change of plan, skipping the master's. I'll do a one-year online critical care fellowship through a UK college instead.
Got a job at Jehangir Hospital in Pune and moved last weekend. Biscuit and Soot took the train like royalty.
Tomasz, 58. Welder at the shipyard in Gdansk, thirty-one years, hull sections mostly.
We live in Przymorze, panel block, fourth floor, with a view of other panel blocks. Very romantic.
My wife Halina teaches Polish at a primary school.
Skoda Octavia estate, 2011, diesel, 240 thousand km and still going.
Type 2 diabetes since 2022. Not fun but you get used to it.
Metformin, twice a day, with food. The pill box lives on the fridge.
Black tea with lemon, no sugar, five glasses a day. The shipyard runs on tea, not steel.
Saturdays I fish at Lake Raduńskie with my brother Marek. We catch mostly silence.
Marek is a taxi driver in Gdynia, twenty years now.
Tram number 6 to the shipyard gate every morning. Shift starts at six so I'm up at 4:45.
I still smoke, about ten a day. Halina nags, I nod.
Our son Kuba studies civil engineering in Wroclaw, third year.
Lunch is the canteen with my crew. Friday is pork cutlet and nobody dares skip it.
Evenings I play chess on the bench outside our block with old Pan Edek, the caretaker. He cheats.
Putting money aside for a small camper van for when I retire. Halina already picked the curtains.
Our dachshund Burek is nine, deaf as a post, thinks he's a Rottweiler.
My phone is an old Nokia with buttons. Don't tell me about touch screens.
HbA1c came back at 7.1. Doctor was cautiously pleased, so I celebrated with an extra cutlet.
Ten days in Croatia on Hvar with Halina, first real holiday in four years.
The Octavia finally died on the S6. Bought a used Passat from a guy in Tczew, 2013, also diesel.
Day 40 without a cigarette. Don't congratulate me, I'm in a terrible mood.
They took me off the torch. Welding inspector now, clipboard instead of electrode, my hands don't know what to do.
Doctor stopped the metformin, I'm on insulin glargine at night now. Needle every evening, fine.
Halina forced a smartphone on me. The Nokia is retired to the drawer with my old watch.
Burek has a girlfriend now. We took in a shelter mutt called Lola.
Knee operation went fine but no more standing in the cold at the lake. I build model ships in the cellar on Saturdays now.
Passat's gone, a truck hit us at the roundabout. Driving Halina's old Fiat Panda until the insurance pays.
Retired this Friday. Thirty-two years, they gave me a cake and a plaque. The 6th tram will run without me.
Bought the camper! A 2008 Fiat Ducato, one owner, smells of pine. The savings jar is empty.
Sold the flat and moved to a little house in Kolbudy with a garden. Burek is confused, Halina is thrilled.
I'm Amara, 29. I run a tailoring shop in Yaba, Lagos, three sewing machines and a cutting table that eats my back.
Home is a two-bedroom flat in Surulere, third floor, generator noise included free.
Two apprentices, Bisi and Kelechi. Bisi is quick, Kelechi is... enthusiastic.
Surulere to Yaba is danfo then keke, an hour on a good day, two when God is busy.
My little brother Chidi lives in Kano, he's a bank teller, only calls when he needs money.
Tecno Camon 18, cracked screen, I refuse to replace it, it still photographs my clients' dresses fine.
Allergic to shellfish. Found out at a wedding in Ikoyi and spent the reception at a clinic. No pork either, just personal.
Afrobeats on speaker all day in the shop. Asake, Ayra Starr, Rema. My apprentices sing louder than the radio.
Saturday choir practice at the Redeemed church in Surulere, then Sunday service. I'm second soprano.
Mum lives in Ibadan, I call her every evening around 8. She always asks if I've eaten.
Doctor said anaemia, so I'm taking iron tablets every morning with orange juice.
My boyfriend Emeka is a civil engineer in Abuja. We see each other once a month when flights allow.
Thursdays I go to Balogun market for fabric. Same three sellers, I know all their children's names.
Saving for an industrial embroidery machine, around 1.2 million naira. I've got maybe a third.
Morning walks, five kilometres round the Teslim Balogun stadium before the sun gets nasty.
The shop is painted yellow, on Herbert Macaulay Way, next to the old bank. Impossible to miss.
I speak Yoruba and English, and my pidgin is first class.
Just back from a week at a fabric expo in Dubai. I touched real silk and may have cried a bit.
My Tecno finally gave up, died in the middle of a fitting. Got a used iPhone 11 from a guy in Computer Village.
Doctor did my blood again, iron is fine now. No more tablets, I'm free.
Learning French on Duolingo, I want to buy fabric directly in Cotonou.
Bisi has graduated from apprentice. She's opened her own stall in Mushin with my blessing and one of my old machines.
Emeka proposed at Jabi Lake!!! I said yes before he finished the sentence.
Moved the shop out of Yaba. Bigger unit in Ikeja, finally a proper cutting table and a changing room for clients.
My knee said stop, so no more walking round the stadium. I do dance workout videos in the living room now.
Forget the embroidery machine for now. The Ikeja rent ate that money and I'm at peace with it.
Married! Small ceremony in Ibadan, Mum cried more than me.
Closed the Ikeja shop and moved to Abuja to live with my husband. Surulere, I'll miss your noise a little bit.
Hiroshi, 67. Retired from Panasonic last year, quality control, thirty-eight years of staring at tiny defects.
My house is in Suita, Osaka. Two storeys, thirty years of creaking floors.
My wife Keiko died three years ago. Some mornings I still put out two cups.
Since then I live alone. The quiet in the house is quite loud.
Every morning I walk the Yamada river for an hour with my Shiba, Shiro.
The doctor has me on amlodipine, 5 mg every morning with breakfast, for blood pressure.
I drive a 2012 Prius, only to the supermarket and the clinic. Like an old man should.
Wednesday afternoons are shogi at the community centre. I get beaten by a ten-year-old.
Daughter Emi works at a bank in Tokyo and rings on Sundays, without fail.
My phone is a flip phone and I love it. Emi says it's a museum piece.
Shiro gets a hip injection every month at Dr. Tanaka's clinic. 7000 yen a time. Worth every yen.
Six pots of tomatoes and cucumbers on the veranda. The cucumbers are winning.
Shiro is thirteen now. Red Shiba, terrible temper, terrible hips.
My son Daichi is an engineer in Nagoya. I see him at Obon and sometimes New Year.
Saturday evening I walk to the sento down the road. Long soak, then a beer from the vending machine.
I speak Japanese and a bit of Korean from my years working in Busan.
Back from five days in Hokkaido with my old Panasonic colleagues. Too much crab.
I'd like to see Lisbon before my knees quit, so I put a little aside every month.
Doctor swapped my amlodipine for losartan. My ankles were like balloons.
Handed in my driving licence at the police station today. Sold the Prius to a very polite young man.
Emi sent me a smartphone and now I'm on LINE. The flip phone lives in a drawer with my Walkman.
English conversation class at the library, Tuesdays. My accent is a crime but the teacher is kind.
Shiro died this morning, in his bed. Fourteen years. I can't write more tonight.
Tomatoes kept dying on me, so the veranda is chrysanthemums only now.
Lost eight kilos and the doctor took me off the blood pressure pills altogether.
Sold the house and moved to a condo in Nishinomiya, with a lift! Farewell Wednesday shogi, farewell sento down the road. My knees send their thanks.
A widow from my old shogi club, Yumiko, and I have started having dinner together. Don't tell Emi yet.
Dropped Lisbon, too many hills. Booked Okinawa for November instead.
Yumiko moved in with me last weekend. Two cups in the morning again.
Soy Lucia, 41. I own a little panaderia called La Concha Dorada in Colonia Roma, Mexico City. We start baking at four in the morning.
I live in my late abuela's house in Coyoacan, the one with the lemon tree that drops fruit on everyone.
My husband Rafael teaches physics at a prepa. He explains proofing dough with thermodynamics and I want to throw things.
Valeria is nine and plays striker for a girls' football team. Saturday matches at nine sharp.
Saturday mornings Rafael and I do the Coyoacan market together. It's the one hour of the week we actually talk.
Every Sunday Rafael and I take Valeria to lunch at his mother's in Iztapalapa. Mole, three hours, no escape.
We have a chihuahua mix called Canela.
Canela is seven, terrified of thunder, and sleeps on my side of the bed.
I drive a 2014 Nissan March to the bakery. At 4 a.m. the whole city is mine.
Flour comes from Molino San Juan every Tuesday morning. If the truck is late I get anxiety rashes.
My head baker is Don Chuy, 62. Eight years with me, he knows the oven better than I do.
Alarm goes off at 3:30 every morning. I don't need coffee, I need a miracle.
Trying to eat low-carb. Which, for a baker, is humiliating.
I swim Tuesday and Thursday evenings at the Deportivo, six o'clock. It's the only quiet I get.
I still owe 200,000 pesos on the new deck oven. Four more years of payments, but she's beautiful.
iPhone SE with a cracked corner and a case made of flour.
I speak Spanish and English, and I'm told my accent in both is very chilanga.
My sister Ana owns a bakery too, in Puebla. We compete over who has the sourer customers.
Long weekend in Puebla for my cousin's quinceanera. I ate three cemitas and regret nothing.
Rent in the Roma doubled, so La Concha Dorada moved to a space in Narvarte. Same smell, different street.
Started Italian lessons online. My abuelo was from Bologna and left a notebook of recipes I can't read.
The March's gearbox gave up right in front of the bakery. Bought a used Kia Rio, don't tell Rafael how much.
Week in Madrid at a baking expo. Ate better churros than mine, I'm furious and inspired.
Gave up the low-carb thing. I'm a baker, I eat bread, end of story.
Pool's behind me now. I run in Viveros de Coyoacan at dawn on my day off with my neighbour Paty.
Paid off the oven! Last instalment cleared today. Rafael bought me a cake from a rival bakery as a joke.
Dropped my iPhone SE into the dough mixer. Samsung A54 now, surviving so far.
Valeria quit football. She's all in on the violin now, apparently Saturdays are for Vivaldi.
Rafael and I have separated. He moved out to his brother's in Narvarte on Sunday. I'm okay, mostly.
Closed La Concha Dorada for good on Saturday. Sold the ovens, hugged Don Chuy and gave him a fat envelope. I start at a culinary school as a teacher next week.
Hi, Ben, 19. First year Geography at Manchester, mostly because I liked field trips at school and hated maths.
I'm from Leeds, parents are still in Horsforth, same house since the day I was born.
I'm in halls in Fallowfield, a room with a window that looks onto the bin store. Romantic.
Dinner is in the halls dining room most nights. The Friday fish is a war crime.
From my halls it's a ten minute walk to lectures, which is the only reason I'm ever on time.
I do weekends at the Tesco Express on Wilmslow Road, twelve hours, minimum wage and a meal deal discount.
My mate Callum works at the Co-op on Oxford Road, we compare staff discounts like absolute dorks.
Vegan since freshers week. Mostly for the planet, a bit for a girl, I'll admit.
My laptop is an ancient Lenovo ThinkPad from sixth form held together with electrical tape and denial.
Hannah, my girlfriend, is at Leeds Uni, we've been together since Year 12.
every night at ten we facetime, even if we are just watching each other eat toast
Hannah comes over every other weekend and sleeps on my floor. The guy next door thinks we're doing something illegal.
Wednesdays I play for the uni's fourth football team. We have lost nine out of nine.
I dont drink coffee. Monster Ultra, the white one, is my entire personality.
Callum's in the same halls as me, floor above, and he plays the bongos at midnight. Send help.
Joined the chess society, Monday nights. I'm bad but they let me stay.
Okay, vegan's dead. Halloumi won. I'm just vegetarian now and I've made my peace with it.
Home in Leeds for Christmas, Mum has put me in the box room again.
Parents' house is a 1930s semi, my old bedroom is now Mum's yoga room, there's a mat where my bed was.
Tore my ankle ligaments in the 9-0 defeat, so that's football finished for me.
Hannah ended it. Said we've become different people. I didn't see it coming.
Turned 20 and Dad got me a MacBook Air. The ThinkPad gets a Viking funeral.
Revision week and I discovered flat whites. Monster Ultra is dead to me.
Switched to Urban Planning, paperwork finally done. The Geography lot waved me off like it was a funeral.
Picked up Saturday shifts on the front desk at the climbing wall, same pay as Tesco but nicer people.
Quit Tesco. Pulling pints in the Northern Quarter on weekend nights now, my feet hate me.
Eating fish again so I'm officially pescatarian. Don't tell the vegans.
Moved into a four-person house in Withington today. Boxes everywhere, one bathroom, already a rota.
I'm Fatima, 36, a pharmacist at a private hospital in Heliopolis. Nine years in the same basement pharmacy, I know every drug rep by their cologne.
We live in Maadi, fourth floor, a flat with a balcony facing a tree that's older than me.
I drive to Heliopolis, thirty-five minutes if the ring road is kind, ninety if it's a Tuesday.
Every second Friday I take the night shift at the hospital, so Karim has to handle the kids.
My husband Karim is a first officer at EgyptAir. Away half the month, jet-lagged the other half.
Our son Yassin is five and goes to a nursery in Maadi. He calls it his office.
I drive a Hyundai Elantra, 2018, silver, with a Lego brick permanently wedged in the air vent.
Turkish coffee, mazbout, medium sugar. Two cups before noon or I'm dangerous.
Zumba on Thursday evenings at the sporting club, the only hour nobody can reach me.
I've had asthma since I was a kid. Ventolin lives in every handbag I own.
Spring is the worst, the khamsin dust sits right on my chest.
My sister Mona is a pharmacist as well, in Alexandria. We compete over who has the more annoying customers.
Doing 16:8 intermittent fasting. Please don't offer me koshary before noon.
I bake birthday cakes for friends and family. The last one was a three-tier unicorn. Never again.
I speak Arabic, English and school French.
Our baby Laila turns one next month and has strong opinions about shoes.
iPhone 11. It's fine. Please don't tell me about newer ones.
Week in Hurghada with the kids. Yassin refuses to get out of the water.
Karim's brother Hany lives in Dubai and keeps sending photos of his pool.
Yassin's first week of Grade 1 at a school in Maadi. He cried at drop-off, I cried in the car.
Opened my own pharmacy on Road 9 in Maadi. Signed the lease, painted the sign myself. Goodbye, basement, after nine years.
Doctor told me to cut sugar, so my Turkish coffee is saada now. Plain. Tragic.
Started Spanish on an app, I want to survive Barcelona next year.
Traded the Elantra for a used Kia Sportage, I needed room for two car seats and delivery boxes for the pharmacy.
Karim got his fourth stripe! Captain now. He wore the uniform to breakfast.
Abandoned the fasting, I was snapping at the staff. Breakfast is back.
No more cakes, I'm doing a pottery class on Wednesdays now. My bowls look like hats.
New Samsung S24. My iPhone went to my mother-in-law.
We're moving to Dubai! Karim's new base. Sold the pharmacy to my cousin Hesham, sold the car, shipping three suitcases and two kids.
Sipho, 45. I drive long-haul for a freight company, Joburg to Durban and Maputo mostly. Twenty years behind the wheel.
The truck is a Scania R460, white, and I treat her better than my back deserves.
I'm on the road Monday to Friday. Home on weekends, if the border behaves.
Company medical aid covers the whole family. That's the only reason I haven't quit.
We live in Orlando East, Soweto, in the house my father built in 1978. Stoep, peach tree, the lot.
My wife Nomsa is a nurse. She gets more respect than me and also more money.
My brother Vusi drives for Imperial. We meet at the Beitbridge border sometimes and share pap.
Lindiwe is in Grade 11 at Orlando High, she wants to study law. God help the magistrates.
Saturday mornings I coach Thandi's under-13 soccer side. We've won one game and the snacks are the best part.
Took the whole family to Durban for the holidays, first time Thandi saw the sea. Sand in everything now.
Kaizer Chiefs season tickets at FNB with Vusi. We suffer together.
My own bakkie is a 2008 Hilux, white, with a dent I'll fix one day.
I smoke about a pack of Peter Stuyvesant a week. Nomsa is a nurse, you can imagine the lectures.
Doctor says my blood pressure is high, I take enalapril every morning. Salt is my enemy now.
I haven't touched alcohol in five years. A truck driver can't afford to.
Our stokvel, twelve of us, everyone puts in R1000 a month and we rotate the payout. Very serious business.
Zulu at home, Sotho from my mum, English at work and a bit of Portuguese from the Maputo runs.
Picked up some Xitsonga from a guy on the Maputo run. He taught me the swear words first.
Samsung A12, screen cracked in a lovely spiderweb.
Nomsa works nights in the maternity ward, so half our marriage happens on WhatsApp.
Nomsa and I went to Sun City for our anniversary. Two nights, and I lost money on only one slot machine.
Doctor stopped the enalapril. Now it's one combination pill, same time every morning.
Hilux's engine blew on the N1. Bought a used Ford Ranger on finance, tell no one how much.
Retrenched on Friday. Twenty years, one letter, a handshake from HR. I'm okay. I'm not okay.
Our stokvel put the contribution up to R1500 a month. Inflation doesn't care about my feelings.
Finally replaced the cracked A12 with a second-hand Redmi. My fingers are very grateful.
New Year's Eve at Vusi's, I had a beer. Then a few more. Five years gone, I'm not proud.
Sold the Ranger, couldn't carry the finance. No vehicle of my own until I'm back on my feet.
Stopped smoking. Nomsa stuck a printed picture of lungs on the fridge and, annoyingly, it worked.
We're going back to Mthatha, my mother's land. I start driving a municipal bus there, Lindiwe starts a new school Monday, and the hired truck leaves Saturday.
Karin, 52. I teach history and religion at a gymnasium in Sundbyberg, twenty-one years of explaining the Thirty Years' War to people who'd rather be asleep.
I bike to school, twenty-five minutes, and in deep winter I give in and take the tunnelbana.
We rent a flat in Bromma, third floor, a hyresratt I got in the nineties and will defend with my life.
My husband Lars is a carpenter. Our flat has three of his shelves, one of which is crooked on purpose, he says.
Every July Lars and I go to our little stuga in the Roslagen archipelago. No wifi, one sauna, bliss.
Friday is tacos at home, Lars does the guacamole, I do the cheese. It's the one tradition the kids still show up for.
Sixten is our cat, a Norwegian forest cat with the dignity of a retired diplomat.
Our son Anton is 24 and works in Malmo at a logistics firm.
Elsa, our daughter, is 21 and studies biology in Uppsala.
I drive a 2009 Volvo V70 that Lars keeps alive out of pure spite.
I knit, mostly sweaters, currently a Fair Isle one for Elsa that she doesn't know about.
Tuesday evenings: choir at Bromma church. Alto, which means I hold the harmony nobody notices.
Coffee, four cups a day. Fika at ten and at three, no matter what the school schedule says.
Iron tablets every morning, my ferritin was low and my doctor believes in them more than I do.
I put 8,000 kronor a month into my ISK account. Pension anxiety in a convenient package.
Swedish, English, and my school German, which is better than I admit.
My sister Ulla teaches at a school in Gothenburg. Same job, different accent.
Weekend in Copenhagen for Elsa's birthday. Too much cake and a very long walk.
Saturday mornings I walk from the flat down to Lake Malaren with a thermos, alone, like a true Swede.
New term, new school. They moved me to Kista, forty minutes each way by train and bus. The principal called it a fresh start.
We adopted a second cat, a tiny grey one called Saga. Sixten is not speaking to us.
Italian lessons on Wednesday evenings, I want to read Dante before I turn sixty.
Lars finally let the V70 die. We bought a used Kia e-Niro and the silence is spooky.
Blood test says my ferritin is fine so no more iron tablets.
Shoulder is wrecked, no more knitting. I paint watercolours now, badly and happily.
Left teaching after twenty-one years. I'm a museum educator at the Historiska now, school groups and no exams to grade.
Lars and I are separating. It's calm and sad and long overdue. He's moved to his sister's in Nacka.
Doubled my pension savings, 12,000 a month into the ISK now. I got scared.
Sixten died last night, he was sixteen. Saga keeps looking for him.
Moved into a one-bedroom on Sodermalm last weekend. New postcode, new life, I barely know where the bins are.
Soy Diego, 31. Line cook at a parrilla in Palermo, grill station. I smell like smoke even in my dreams.
I work Tuesday to Saturday, 4 p.m. to 1 a.m. My social life is a Monday.
I take the 29 colectivo to Palermo, forty minutes, reading on my phone and missing my stop at least once a week.
We live in Boedo, a one-bedroom on the second floor with a balcony that fits exactly one chair.
My girlfriend Camila is a vet. She can calm a rottweiler but not my mother.
Pancho is our dog, a mutt with one ear up and zero concept of personal space.
Sunday asado at Camila's parents' place in Quilmes. Her dad guards the grill like a border.
Peanut allergy, the dangerous kind. I carry an EpiPen even though I'm a cook. Especially because I'm a cook.
First reaction was at a birthday party when I was eight. ER visit, nobody forgot.
I'm a Boca socio, La Bombonera every other Sunday. Don't ask me to explain, it's a religion.
Crossfit at 11 a.m. before my shift, three times a week. My coach calls my form creative.
Mate, around ten a day. The thermos is basically attached to my hand.
My brother Nico drives a remis in Caballito. He thinks cooking is a hobby.
I keep my savings in dollars in a tin behind the pasta. Everybody does.
Spanish and Italian, my nonna was from Calabria and swore at me in it.
Five-year plan: open my own restaurant. Ten tables, one grill, no menu in English.
Flew to Montevideo for a friend's wedding. So much dulce de leche I'm in danger.
Cooked at a pop-up in Mendoza for a week. Hands full of burns and wine.
Camila's sister Flor lives in Boedo too, three blocks away, and she borrows my tools.
Learning English with a podcast, I want to read the cookbooks in the original.
Left the parrilla. New pasta kitchen in Almagro, ten minutes on foot from my door, nine to five, and nobody shouts. I don't trust it.
Gave back my Boca socio card, too expensive and the team's a mess.
Camila and I are done. She took Pancho, I took two suitcases.
Six weeks on Nico's couch in Caballito now. His fridge is a crime scene.
Signed a lease on a studio in San Telmo! Tiny, cobblestones, a landlady who talks to herself.
Quit the kitchen. I have my own food truck now, choripan and provoleta at Parque Lezama, drowning in paperwork.
Moved my dollars out of the tin into a bank account. My mother made me.
Cut down the mate, doctor says my stomach is shot. Tea. I'm sorry, tea.
Ditched crossfit, too expensive. Now I run along the Costanera Sur at dawn.
Scrapped the restaurant dream. A truck is enough, less debt and nobody to call at 2 a.m.
Kai, 28. I'm a sparky on a mine site near Newman, FIFO out of Perth. The hi-vis tan lines are real.
Roster is two weeks on, one week off. Two weeks of dust, one week of pretending to be a normal person.
Flights out of Perth airport at 5 a.m. on changeover day. The 4 a.m. alarm makes me violent.
On site I'm in a donga, room 214, sharing a bathroom with a bloke who snores through walls.
When I'm off I'm back at my parents' place in Rockingham, saving every cent.
I train at the Rockingham gym on my week off. Shoulders and back, the usual bro fare.
Every off-week morning it's a flat white and a toastie at the cafe on Kent Street. Same order, the barista knows.
My girlfriend Mia is a primary school teacher in Joondalup. Seven months in and she tolerates my snoring.
Ute is a Ford Ranger, 2019, grey. My pride and my biggest debt.
I've got a kelpie called Dusty, six years old, lives at Mum and Dad's and thinks the garden is his.
Dusty swims better than I do. Jumps off the jetty at Rockingham every chance he gets.
Surf at Secret Harbour whenever the swell isn't pathetic.
Started fishing off the Rockingham jetty with Dad on Sundays.
Mia's brother Tom is a sparky too, in Geraldton. We argue about cable sizes at Christmas.
My mate Brodie works at the same mine, different crew. We share the smoko hut sometimes.
I have a few tinnies every off-week, mostly Gold, mostly at the pub with Brodie.
Right shoulder's cooked from overhead cable work. Can't lift anything above my head without a groan.
Mia and I are saving for a house deposit, 60k each by the end of next year, if interest rates behave.
iPhone 14. Does the job and the screen's miraculously intact.
A week in Bali for Brodie's 30th. I surfed, he fell off a scooter, we're both fine.
Transferred to the gas plant at Karratha. New site, new roster, eight days on and six off.
Proposed to Mia on the Fremantle Esplanade. She said yes and then laughed for ten minutes.
Shoulder's finally healed after physio and a lot of boring exercises. Lifting overhead like it's 2020.
Haven't had a beer since September. My sleep is unreal and my wallet is thrilled.
Sold the Ranger, couldn't justify the repayments. Picked up a 2016 Subaru Outback. Boring and brilliant.
Quit FIFO. Starting Monday as a local sparky for a company in Fremantle. I get to sleep in my own bed every night, it feels illegal.
Mia and I moved in together, a rental in Fremantle near the markets. Dusty's staying with Mum for now and sulking.
We got married! Backyard wedding at Mum and Dad's, Dusty was ring bearer for about ten seconds.
Dropped my iPhone off the jetty. Pixel 9 now, Mia says it's karma.
We got a second dog, a pug called Nugget. Dusty is unimpressed.
Walter, 75, retired machinist. Forty-one years at the same plant in Dayton. My hands still twitch when I hear a lathe.
We live in a brick ranch in Kettering, Ohio. Bought it in 1979 and the porch light's been on ever since.
My wife June and I do the crossword every morning at seven. She does the clues, I do the complaining.
I mow the lawn every Saturday in summer, push mower. A riding mower is for quitters.
Basement workshop, mostly birdhouses and the occasional rocking horse for the grandkids.
Golf Tuesdays and Fridays at the municipal course. I shoot a 95 on a good day.
My neighbour Bob golfs too. He cheats on the scorecard and I let him.
I drive a 2006 Buick LeSabre, 98,000 miles, one owner: me.
Thursday nights I drive to the VFW hall for euchre. Second best in the post.
Wednesday mornings I do the Kroger run with June's list in my shirt pocket.
Low sodium diet since the heart thing. Food tastes like cardboard that's been to church.
Doctor wants me under 1,500 mg a day. I read labels like they owe me money.
I take warfarin and get my INR checked every month at the clinic.
Folgers, black, five cups a day. Doctor says it's fine, June says it's a lifestyle.
Our daughter Beth lives in Columbus, she's a nurse with two kids and drives down once a month.
Our son Greg lives in Phoenix. Calls on Sundays, from the car, always from the car.
My phone is a Jitterbug flip phone with big buttons. June handles the texting.
I listen to every Reds game on the radio on the porch, even when it hurts, which is often.
I walk laps at the Dayton Mall at 8 every morning before the stores open, with the other old guys.
Drove up to Pittsburgh for June's sister's funeral. Six hours each way, sad weekend.
Joined a bridge club on Mondays, June made me.
Hip replacement was Tuesday. Doc says golf is done for me. I'll putt on the living room carpet.
Switched from warfarin to Eliquis. No more monthly needle sticks.
Doctor finally got me. Decaf now. I'm in mourning.
Traded the Buick for a used F-150, my knees can't climb out of a low car anymore.
Beth gave me her old iPhone. June says I text like a teenager, two words at a time.
Cardiologist says my numbers are great. Salt limit is 2,300 now, not 1,500. I salted an egg with tears in my eyes.
Greg moved back to Dayton! New job at Wright-Patt, twelve minutes from our house.
Gave up my driver's licence today. Eyes, reflexes and the DMV lady all agreed. Greg took the truck, and the VFW and Kroger will have to survive without me.
We've moved into Maple Court, the retirement place off Dorothy Lane. No more lawn, no more basement, plenty of bingo.
